title_zh: 输家心态（Loser Mentality）：Matt Levine 对话 Mary Giles——Jensen Huang 间谍婚外情与 Anthropic 上市
subtitle_zh: Matt Levine 与 Mary Giles 复盘 Jensen Huang 婚外情风波、Anthropic IPO，以及 ChatGPT 如何左右散户投资。

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios.
turns.zh: Bloomberg Audio Studios。

turns.en: Podcasts. Radio.
turns.zh: 播客。广播。

turns.en: News.
turns.zh: 新闻。

turns.en: Mary, can you talk?
turns.zh: Mary，你能出声吗？

turns.en: Hey, it's me. See the bunny sleeping. Sorry, it's stuck in my head.
turns.zh: 嘿，是我。'看那只小兔子在睡觉'——抱歉，这句一直在我脑子里转。

turns.en: Hello and welcome to a special Veterans Day edition of the Money Stuff podcast.
turns.zh: 大家好，欢迎收听 Money Stuff 播客的退伍军人节（Veterans Day）特别版。

turns.en: Thank you for your service.
turns.zh: 感谢你们的服役与付出。

turns.en: I'm Matt Levine. I write the Money Stuff column for Bloomberg Opinion. And I'm joined here by... Yeah, hi. Are we going to bleep your name out or are we going to use your name?
turns.zh: 我是 Matt Levine，为 Bloomberg Opinion 撰写 Money Stuff 专栏。今天和我一起的还有……嗯，你好。我们要不要把你的名字消音，还是直接说出来？

turns.en: Can you introduce yourself as, like, largest Levine child?
turns.zh: 你能不能把我介绍成，比如，'Levine 家的大孩子'？

turns.en: Yes, this is my eldest daughter, heir apparent, who's off school for the day. And we're also joined by Mary Giles.
turns.zh: 好，这是我的大女儿，法定继承人，今天学校放假。我们还请到了 Mary Giles。

turns.en: And also me.
turns.zh: 还有我。

turns.en: Hi.
turns.zh: 你好。

turns.en: Host of Married America, available wherever you get your podcasts.
turns.zh: Mary in America 的主持人，在你听播客的任何平台都能收听到。

turns.en: Mary and I have actually podcasted before in a famous lost episode of Planet Money that has never seen the light of day, but.
turns.zh: Mary 和我以前其实一起录过播客，就在那期著名却'失传'、从未见天日的 Planet Money 里，不过……

turns.en: It's really good.
turns.zh: 那期真的很棒。

turns.en: It's really good. I feel like you had an agenda.
turns.zh: 真的很棒。我感觉你是有备而来。

turns.en: He said I could podcast about Zelda, and then he said I couldn't.
turns.zh: 他先说我可以在播客里聊 Zelda，然后又说不能。

turns.en: Why not? I don't know.
turns.zh: 为什么不行？——我不知道。

turns.en: He just said no.
turns.zh: 他就是说不行。

turns.en: I think he's wrong. Go ahead.
turns.zh: 我觉得他错了。你说吧。

turns.en: Do you have some good financial or economic analysis of The Legend of Zelda?
turns.zh: 你对《塞尔达传说》（The Legend of Zelda）有什么像样的金融或经济学分析吗？

turns.en: They use rupees as money.
turns.zh: 他们那儿用卢比（rupees）当钱。

turns.en: I've written in the past about the Pokemon market at your school. Can you explain? So like what I've written is that there is a lot of information asymmetry in the Pokemon market at your school, which is to say that slightly older kids or even not older kids, just more just bolder kids will tell other kids that like their cards are fake or that like these cards are very rare. And I have never believed that. But can you give some insight into like the market structure of Pokemons at your school?
turns.zh: 我以前写过你们学校的宝可梦（Pokémon）市场。你能解释一下吗？我写的是，你们学校的宝可梦市场存在大量信息不对称（information asymmetry），也就是说，稍微大一点的孩子，甚至不是更大、只是更大胆的孩子，会告诉别的孩子说他们的卡是假的，或者说这些卡非常稀有。我一直不太信这套。那你能不能讲讲你们学校宝可梦的市场结构？

turns.en: A real Pokemon for the gold cards. If it has like a smaller ball in the center of the Pokeball, then it's fake. Or if it doesn't have a star at the bottom.
turns.zh: 说到金卡的正版宝可梦：如果精灵球（Pokéball）正中间的球比较小，那就是假的；或者如果底部没有一颗星，也是假的。

turns.en: Whoa.
turns.zh: 哇哦。

turns.en: Have you seen a lot of fake cards? Yeah.
turns.zh: 你见过很多假卡吗？——见过。

turns.en: Our dog just showed up. Ginger wants to be on mic too.
turns.zh: 我们家的狗刚跑过来了。Ginger 也想上麦克风。

turns.en: Good dog. Come here, Ginger.
turns.zh: 好狗狗。过来，Ginger。

turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.en: That's the Pokemon analysis. Here's our dog.
turns.zh: 宝可梦分析就讲到这儿。这是我们的狗。

turns.en: Oh, good dog.
turns.zh: 哦，好狗狗。

turns.en: Ruff, ruff, ruff, ruff, ruff, ruff.
turns.zh: 汪，汪，汪，汪，汪，汪。

turns.en: Good job, Ginger. Thank you for that contribution. Back to Pokemon. I'm not done yet. How many Pokemon cards do you have?
turns.zh: 干得好，Ginger，谢谢你的'贡献'。回到宝可梦——我还没聊完呢。你有多少张宝可梦卡？

turns.en: Well, I gave most of mine to my brothers.
turns.zh: 嗯，我的大部分都给我弟弟们了。

turns.en: You retired. So I have like 20.
turns.zh: 你'退隐'了。所以我大概还剩20张。

turns.en: That's a nest egg.
turns.zh: 那可是笔储备金（nest egg）。

turns.en: Yeah, the Pokemon market is a short-lived one. The way I understand Pokemon is that every child goes through an intense six-month period of really wanting the best Pokemons and being very concerned about having rare Pokemons and collecting and trading Pokemon. And paying attention to Pokemons. And then one day, they're just like, never mind. And they hand the Pokemons to another child. So right now, my daughter has gotten rid of her Pokemons, but my sons have collected them.
turns.zh: 是啊，宝可梦市场是个'昙花一现'的市场。我对宝可梦的理解是，每个孩子都会经历一段为期六个月、非常狂热的阶段，特别想要最好的宝可梦，特别在意有没有稀有宝可梦，收集、交换宝可梦，密切关注宝可梦。然后某一天，他们突然就'算了，无所谓'，把宝可梦转手给另一个孩子。所以现在，我女儿已经处理掉了她的宝可梦，而我儿子们把它们接手了。

turns.en: My contractor who recently, we just renovated a bathroom and our contractor's big in Pokemon. And he told us all about how it has outperformed the S & P. It's outperformed gold. And don't put them in a binder, he said, because it'll crinkle the edges like just a little bit and that will degrade the value in some of them. You can send them off to get truly appraised, but some of them are more valuable if you don't do that. It was a two hour masterclass. And basically my takeaway, not investing advice. He said to go to Target right now, buy a couple bins, put them in plastic storage bins and put them in my attic and not touch them until my children are ready to go to college. And that that will fund all three children's college. Do you think that's good advice?
turns.zh: 我那个承包商——我们最近刚翻新了一个浴室，承包商特别玩宝可梦。他跟我们讲了一大通，说宝可梦的表现跑赢了标普500（S&P），跑赢了黄金。他说别把它们放进活页册（binder），因为那样会让边角稍微起褶，从而折损其中一些卡的价值。你可以寄去做真正的鉴定评级，但有些卡如果你不这么做反而更值钱。那是一场两小时的大师课。基本上我的收获是——不是投资建议啊——他说现在就去 Target，买上几箱，把它们装进塑料收纳箱，放到我家阁楼里，别去碰，一直等到我的孩子们要上大学的时候。那样就能供得起三个孩子上大学。你觉得这是好建议吗？

turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不是。

turns.en: Love you.
turns.zh: 爱你哦。

turns.en: Right. I feel like the Pokemons are for handling and looking at and analyzing how much damage they do and not under any circumstances ever for playing the Pokemon card game.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得宝可梦卡是用来拿在手里、端详、研究它们能造成多少伤害的，任何时候都绝不是用来玩宝可梦卡牌游戏的。

turns.en: That's the least useful way.
turns.zh: 玩游戏是最没用的玩法。

turns.en: I've never met a child who's ever played a Pokemon card game. I once tried and we spent like an hour reading the rules and we got like one quarter of the way through the rules and we're like, nevermind, this is terrible.
turns.zh: 我从没见过哪个孩子真的玩过宝可梦卡牌游戏。我有一次试着玩，我们花了大概一小时读规则，才读了大概四分之一，然后就'算了，这玩意儿太糟了'。

turns.en: No, really?
turns.zh: 不会吧，真的？

turns.en: My sons do not know that there is a game that you can play with Pokemon, although they are very interested in the damage that each Pokemon does, and no one's going to tell them about the game. All right, shall we move on to financial news? Sometimes the mommy and the daddy love each other very much, but also there's a Chinese spy. We're going to talk about that.
turns.zh: 我儿子们根本不知道宝可梦还能拿来玩一个游戏，尽管他们对每只宝可梦能造成多少伤害非常感兴趣，而且谁都不会告诉他们有这么个游戏。好了，我们来聊聊财经新闻吧？有时候爸爸妈妈彼此非常相爱，但另外还冒出来一个中国间谍。我们就要聊这个。

turns.en: No, no.
turns.zh: 别，别。

turns.en: Oh my God. Matt, I specifically put in the show notes to protect her from this.
turns.zh: 天呐。Matt，我特地在节目备注里写了要保护她，别让她碰到这些。

turns.en: We'll see you later. Bye.
turns.zh: 我们回头见。拜拜。

turns.en: The world's worst transition. Let's talk about Jensen.
turns.zh: 这是世界上最生硬的转场。我们来聊聊 Jensen 吧。

turns.en: Hi, this is Matt on Thursday. I'm just jumping in here to say that obviously things went south for Jensen Huang after we recorded this episode. He resigned and I wrote about it on Thursday's Money Stuff newsletter and we might talk about it on the podcast next week. But for now, back to our conversation from Wednesday before that happened.
turns.zh: 大家好，我是周四的 Matt。我插一句：显然，在我们录完这期之后，Jensen Huang 的处境急转直下。他辞职了，我在周四的 Money Stuff 简报里写了这件事，下周的播客里我们可能会聊。但现在，还是回到我们在事情发生之前、周三录的那段对话。

turns.en: I know a lot of people who are heartbroken. People in the AI space who I basically had to send a couple wellness checks out just to make sure they're coping. Oh, heartbroken. They loved him. They feel personally betrayed by him.
turns.zh: 我认识很多心碎的人。AI 圈里那些人，我基本得挨个发去'关怀问候'，确认他们撑不撑得住。哦，真是心碎。他们以前那么喜欢他，现在觉得被他个人背叛了。

turns.en: Wait, there's a.
turns.zh: 等等，有一篇……

turns.en: Wall Street Journal story that quotes a professor at the university in Taiwan saying, he truly is sort of the cool uncle personified in which he would never be the problematic one.
turns.zh: 《华尔街日报》（Wall Street Journal）的报道，引用了台湾一所大学一位教授的话，说他真的就是'那个很酷的叔叔'的化身，永远都不会是那个惹麻烦的人。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: He was the cool uncle. No.
turns.zh: 他就是那个'酷叔叔'。不。

turns.en: He was the cool uncle. He was a real one. He didn't wake up with a loser mentality. Does everyone get that reference? That's a reference to the Dworkesh podcast in which Dworkesh was literally asking about like China getting chips and should we be not selling to China for security reasons? And Jensen's like, that's a loser mentality. And it's a bar, like it's actually so good, but it's like in retrospect.
turns.zh: 他就是那个'酷叔叔'，是个货真价实的酷叔叔。他早上醒来可没有那种'输家心态'（loser mentality）。大家都懂这个梗吗？这指的是 Dwarkesh 那期播客，Dwarkesh 当时就在问，关于中国拿到芯片、出于安全考量我们是不是不该卖给中国这类问题。Jensen 就说，那是'输家心态'。这话说得真够狠的，其实特别精彩，只不过现在回头看……

turns.en: Right. I mean, he's a big deal generally, right? But like, he's like the leading voice for a couple of like important positions in AI, which are very much aligned with his own commercial interests. One of which is like, we should sell chips to China all day long. It's a loser mentality to worry about it. And another one of which is, we should not be pacing the frontier, right? Like the Daryl Amadeus of the world are like, we should be slowing things down.
turns.zh: 对。我是说，他整体上是个大人物，对吧？但他算是 AI 领域几个重要立场上的头号代言人，而这些立场跟他自己的商业利益高度一致。其中之一就是：我们应该没日没夜地往中国卖芯片，担心这事儿是'输家心态'。另一个是：我们不该给前沿（frontier）踩刹车，对吧？像 Dario Amodei 那类人会说，我们应该放慢速度。

turns.en: Please stop me, yeah.
turns.zh: 请拦着我点，是啊。

turns.en: And Jensen Huang is like, That's a loser mentality.
turns.zh: 而 Jensen Huang 会说，那是'输家心态'。

turns.en: That's a loser mentality.
turns.zh: '那是输家心态'。

turns.en: One reason for that could be sincere belief. Another reason for that could be he's selling chips so the faster the frontier is not being paced, the more chips he's selling. Those positions have been undermined by his being caught having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
turns.zh: 一个原因可能是他真的这么信。另一个原因可能是他在卖芯片，所以前沿推进得越不受约束，他卖的芯片就越多。而这些立场，如今因为他被曝出与一名疑似中国间谍有染而受到了削弱。

turns.en: Or whoever she is, a white glove connector professional. Many different types of spies, I've learned.
turns.zh: 或者不管她是谁吧，一个'白手套'式的掮客型人物。我算是学到了，间谍有很多种类型。

turns.en: Nothing relies on her being an actual agent of Chinese intelligence, right? If she is Simply working at a Singaporean neocloud that is smuggling chips to China, that's also bad. And frankly, by the way, even if there's nothing bad and all it is is he's having an affair with a customer, that's not great corporate governance. Someone emailed me like, isn't that a related party transaction that has to be disclosed in their financial statements? Maybe, maybe. It's not great.
turns.zh: 这一切并不取决于她是不是中国情报机构的正式特工，对吧？如果她只是在新加坡一家往中国走私芯片的新型云服务商（neocloud）工作，那也一样糟糕。而且坦白说，退一步讲，就算没什么坏事，仅仅是他跟一个客户有染，那也算不上好的公司治理（corporate governance）。有人给我发邮件说，这难道不是必须在财报里披露的关联方交易（related party transaction）吗？也许吧，也许。总之不太好看。

turns.en: It's not great.
turns.zh: 不太好看。

turns.en: Like, you know, it's obviously a much worse story if she's a spy or even just, you know, involved in smuggling chips to China.
turns.zh: 你知道，如果她是间谍，甚至只是卷入往中国走私芯片，那显然就是糟糕得多的故事了。

turns.en: Is it that much worse? It seems like the smuggling chips to China part, a straight up affair would be like better.
turns.zh: 真有那么糟得多吗？看起来，比起'走私芯片到中国'这部分，单纯的一段婚外情反而还好一些。

turns.en: Oh, sure.
turns.zh: 哦，那当然。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: So like, you know, over the weekend, it sort of came out definitively that Jensen Wang was having an affair with this woman, Alice Wang, who is allegedly involved in Chinese intelligence in some way. but who at least is involved in a company that is.
turns.zh: 所以说，上周末，事情基本上板上钉钉地曝出来了：Jensen Huang 跟一位叫 Alice Wang 的女性有染，据称她以某种方式牵涉中国情报，但至少她所在的公司是牵涉其中的。

turns.en: Singaporean Neocloud.
turns.zh: 一家新加坡的新型云服务商。

turns.en: Yeah, that has been investigated for violating export controls. And so it came out over the weekend that this was happening. He sent out a memo to staff saying, sorry, guys, I did have this. After weeks of saying that his relationship with Megaspeed, which is the Singaporean Neocloud, his relationship with it was normal.
turns.zh: 对，那家公司曾因违反出口管制（export controls）被调查。所以上周末这事儿就曝出来了。他给员工发了一份备忘录说，对不起各位，我确实有这段关系。而在此前的几周里，他一直说，他跟 Megaspeed——就是那家新加坡新型云服务商——之间的关系是'正常'的。

turns.en: Quote, normal, close quote. I love that. They're like, everyone is always doing this. Okay. Haven't you read a single novel? Everyone has affairs.
turns.zh: '正常'，加引号。我太爱这个说法了。他们那架势就像，'大家一直都这么干啊'。拜托，你难道一本小说都没读过吗？谁都有婚外情。

turns.en: This is totally normal. Right. But in any case.
turns.zh: '这完全正常'。对。但不管怎样……

turns.en: This is tale as old as time.
turns.zh: 这是亘古不变的老故事（tale as old as time）。

turns.en: Tale as old as time. But no, he said it was normal. And then he eventually admitted there was an affair. And it took about $ 400 billion off of NVIDIA's market cap for, I think, like good reasons, like good sort of discounted cash flow reasons. Like, One, this is definitely revived calls for like stricter export controls on chips. Two, the board is going to do an investigation, right? They've hired Wachtel Lipton, my old firm, to like write a scaling report.
turns.zh: 亘古不变的老故事。但不，他先说是'正常'，后来才终于承认有婚外情。而这一下子让 NVIDIA 的市值蒸发了大约 4000 亿美元，我觉得是有充分理由的，是从现金流折现（DCF）角度讲得通的理由。其一，这肯定会重新唤起对芯片实施更严格出口管制的呼声。其二，董事会要展开调查，对吧？他们请了 Wachtell Lipton——我的老东家——来出一份报告。

turns.en: Pause. Fun job. Are you so jealous?
turns.zh: 打住。这活儿真有意思。你是不是特嫉妒？

turns.en: Kind of. I'm jealous.
turns.zh: 有点儿。我是挺嫉妒的。

turns.en: Call me, Wachtel.
turns.zh: 打给我啊，Wachtell。

turns.en: I've written about the Wachtel report about Steve Ballmer and getting on the NBA salary cap by like doing weird transactions. That was a cool job. This is like a little Todd.
turns.zh: 我写过 Wachtell 那份关于 Steve Ballmer、讲他如何靠一些奇怪交易来规避 NBA 工资帽的报告。那活儿很酷。这次这个嘛，就稍微'小'了一点。

turns.en: Pablo Torre kind of did that also, to be fair.
turns.zh: 说句公道话，Pablo Torre 也算干过那种事。

turns.en: Yeah, yeah, sure, sure, sure. That was Palo Torre first and then Wagtail. And this one is like, you know, the CIA first and then Wagtail.
turns.zh: 对对对，没错没错。那次是 Pablo Torre 先上，然后才轮到 Wachtell。而这次呢，是中情局（CIA）先上，然后才轮到 Wachtell。

turns.en: Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 对对对对。

turns.en: But so they're going to do this report and then like they're going to hand it to the board. And as fiduciaries for shareholders, there's like a background question of like the board should probably have thought more about making the company robust to the loss of its, you know, visionary chief executive officer who has 50 direct reports and works all the time and is identified so prominently with the company. Probably the board should have thought, you know, five or 10 years ago, hey, we need a deeper bench. We need some succession planning. We need to be confident.
turns.zh: 所以说，他们会做这份报告，然后交给董事会。而作为股东的受托人（fiduciary），这里有个背景层面的问题：董事会本该更多地考虑，如何让公司在失去它那位富有远见的 CEO 时依然稳健——这位 CEO 有 50 个直接下属、无时无刻不在工作，而且跟公司形象深度绑定。董事会大概早在五年前、十年前就该想：嘿，我们需要更深厚的人才梯队（bench），需要做继任计划（succession planning），需要有信心。

turns.en: That's loser mentality.
turns.zh: 那才是'输家心态'呢。

turns.en: Right. It's easy for me to say that, right? It's not obvious that it's easy for them to do it, right? I mean, he is a.
turns.zh: 对。我这么说是很容易的，对吧？但对它们来说要做到可没那么容易，对吧？我是说，他毕竟是个……

turns.en: No, but that is dork stuff. Like we talked one time about like the old world of these stuff. rules and boards selecting successions and da-da-da-da-da. And, like, I used the example of Artsy being, like, totally enamored with its founders' increasingly Burning Man, like, wild missives. And it's the same... To me, it feels the same, where it's like, yeah, we have this genius. Let's build the whole thing around him. He is the thing. And to dilute that and become the stodgy, like more responsible version is way less profitable.

turns.en: But so anyway, a PhD student at NYU named Valerie Baldinger has a paper on generative AI and retail investment, where she used data from a wealth management platform serving US retail investors that introduced an assistant based on ChatGPT and Gemini in November 2024. So she just looked at what the chatbot told the customers to do and then what the customers did. And she found that they all bought index funds. Like the chatbot was like, you should buy index funds. And the customers were like, okay, we'll buy index funds. And so it improved their performance and reduced their risk because it was just giving them the standard advice and they were listening to it, which there's a lot of interesting things there. One is like, it's not any of the weird stories. It's the boring story of like, they told people the right answer or the normal answer and they did it. Normal answer. Another thing that's fascinating about it is like, It's not just that it told them to do it, it's that they did it. And her claim is that the mechanism is that it gave them very personalized advice. It was like, well, here are the stocks that you have, and here are the risks of the stocks that you have, and so buy index funds. And so what I love about it is I've thought for years there's this belief in the wealth advisory world that people are different and you should give people differentiated financial advice based on their circumstances and risk tolerance. And I've always thought, one... Everyone wants the same thing, which is stocks that go up. And two, in a more realistic world where there's a risk-reward trade-off, there's a right answer, which is long-term index fund ownership. And it would be kind of weird if it was actually useful to give people personalized advice. Because what you want is stocks that go up rather than some weird niche thing. But anyway, the point is that ChatGPT correctly threaded that needle and gave people personalized advice that always told them the same thing, which is buy index funds.
turns.zh: 总之，NYU 一位叫 Valerie Baldinger 的博士生写了一篇关于生成式 AI（generative AI）与散户投资的论文。她用的数据来自一家服务美国散户的财富管理平台，该平台在 2024 年 11 月上线了一个基于 ChatGPT 和 Gemini 的助手。她只是观察了聊天机器人告诉客户去做什么、以及客户实际做了什么。结果她发现，所有人都买了指数基金。就是说，聊天机器人说'你该买指数基金'，客户就说'好，那我们买指数基金'。于是它改善了他们的收益、降低了他们的风险，因为它给的就是那套标准建议，而客户听了。这里面有很多有意思的点。其一，它不是任何一种古怪的故事，而是那个'无聊'的故事：它们告诉了人们正确的、或者说常规的答案，而人们照做了——常规的答案。另一件迷人之处是，不只是它告诉他们去做，而是他们真的去做了。她的论点是，机制在于它给出了非常个性化的建议，比如：'这是你持有的股票，这是你所持股票的风险，所以你该买指数基金。'我之所以特别喜欢这点，是因为多年来我一直认为，财富咨询界有一种信念，觉得每个人都不一样，你应当根据他们的处境和风险承受能力给出差异化的理财建议。而我一直觉得：第一，每个人想要的其实是同一件事，就是会涨的股票；第二，在一个更现实、存在风险—收益权衡的世界里，是有一个正确答案的，那就是长期持有指数基金。如果'给人个性化建议'真的有用，那反而有点奇怪，因为你想要的是会涨的股票，而不是某种古怪的小众玩意儿。但总之，关键在于 ChatGPT 精准地穿过了这根针眼：它给出了个性化建议，而这些建议永远告诉人们同一件事——买指数基金。
